> On Feb 16, 2017, at 2:41 PM, Jan Münch <jan.lenna...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> Hey Stan Group,
> I am new to Bayes and try to apply it in the next month to some hidden Markov model inference for proteins. Sofar my toy triexponential decay model does not behave well.
> R_hat goes to inifity even though my Priors are to my understanding really restrictive what am I doing wrong here? The rates are seperated by an order of Magnitude. So they should be distinguishabel...
>
> regress_code_simple = """
> data {
> int<lower = 0> N; // number of observations
> real counts[N]; // response variable
> real time[N]; // predictor variable
> }
> parameters {
> real<lower=0> rate1;
> real<lower=rate1> rate2;
> real<lower=rate2> rate3;

Easier to just do

positive_ordered[3] rate;

> real<lower=0> sigma; // standard deviation
> }
> transformed parameters {
> real mu[N]; // fitted values
> for(i in 1:N)
> mu[i] = 0.4*exp(-rate1*time[i])+3.0/10*exp(-rate2*time[i])+3.0/10*exp(-rate3*time[i]);

This can be vectorized as follows:

mu = 0.4 * exp(-rate1 * time)
+ 0.3 * exp(-rate2 * time)
+ 0.3 * exp(-rate3 * time));

if you declare time as a vector:

vector[N] time;

But the bigger problem is that it's not going to be identified because
you've introduced essentially three regression-like coefficient based
on the same coefficient and you've given the first two rates plenty of
latitude.

> }
> model {
> real alpha;
> real beta;
> alpha = 1.0;
> beta = 1.0;
>
>
>
> sigma ~ gamma(alpha,beta);

Much better to just do

sigma ~ gamma(1, 1);

>
> rate1 ~ normal(0,5)T[0,];
> rate2 ~ normal(9,5)T[0,];
> rate3 ~ normal(95,10)T[0,];

This isn't the right truncations to normalize:

rate[1] ~ normal(0, 5) T[0, ];
rate[2] ~ normal(9, 5) T[rate[1], 0];
rate[3] ~ normal(95, 10) T[rate[2], 0];

You can drop the first truncation for efficiency, but you need
the next two because they depend on parameters.

> counts ~ normal(mu,sigma);

But I have no idea why you'd do this. If you want to define a mixture,
I'd suggest looking at the mixture modeling section of the manual. You
mix the whole distributions, not the means.

> }
> """
> The error analysis is bad at the beginning and then is fine for some time

The only parameters that look OK here are the rate and sigma. You may have
numerical issues in the mu leading to underflow and overflow with the exp(),
but I'm guessing you really meant to implement a mixture model, not something
with an odd composite mean.

- Bob

mu[0] ~ normal(1,1)T[0, ];

Exception thrown at line 14: []: accessing element out of range. index 0 out of range; expecting index to be between 1 and 3; index position = 1mu

Hope this helps!

> Hey Stan Group,
> I am new to Bayes and try to apply it in the next month to some hidden Markov model inference for proteins. Sofar my toy triexponential decay model does not behave well.
>  R_hat goes to inifity even though my Priors are to my understanding really restrictive what am I doing wrong here? The rates are seperated by an order of Magnitude. So they should be distinguishabel...

> regress_code_simple = """
> data {
>  int<lower = 0> N; // number of observations

>  real time[N]; // predictor variable
> }
> parameters {
>  real<lower=0> rate1;
>  real<lower=rate1> rate2;
>  real<lower=rate2> rate3;

Easier to just do

  positive_ordered[3] rate;

>  real<lower=0> sigma; // standard deviation
> }
> transformed parameters {
>  real mu[N]; // fitted values
> for(i in 1:N)
>  mu[i] = 0.4*exp(-rate1*time[i])+3.0/10*exp(-rate2*time[i])+3.0/10*exp(-rate3*time[i]);

This can be vectorized as follows:

  mu = 0.4 * exp(-rate1 * time)
     + 0.3 * exp(-rate2 * time)
     + 0.3 * exp(-rate3 * time));

if you declare time as a vector:

  vector[N] time;

But the bigger problem is that it's not going to be identified because
you've introduced essentially three regression-like coefficient based
on the same coefficient and you've given the first two rates plenty of
latitude.

> }
> model {
>  real alpha;
>  real beta;
>  alpha = 1.0;
>  beta  = 1.0;
>
>
>
>  sigma ~ gamma(alpha,beta);

Much better to just do

  sigma ~ gamma(1, 1);

>
>  rate1 ~ normal(0,5)T[0,];
>  rate2 ~ normal(9,5)T[0,];
>  rate3 ~ normal(95,10)T[0,];

This isn't the right truncations to normalize:

  rate[1] ~ normal(0, 5) T[0, ];
  rate[2] ~ normal(9, 5) T[rate[1], 0];
  rate[3] ~ normal(95, 10) T[rate[2], 0];

You can drop the first truncation for efficiency, but you need
the next two because they depend on parameters.

>  counts ~ normal(mu,sigma);

But I have no idea why you'd do this.  If you want to define a mixture,
I'd suggest looking at the mixture modeling section of the manual.  You
mix the whole distributions, not the means.


> }
> """
> The error analysis is bad at the beginning and then is fine for some time

The only parameters that look OK here are the rate and sigma.  You may have
numerical issues in the mu leading to underflow and overflow with the exp(),
but I'm guessing you really meant to implement a mixture model, not something
with an odd composite mean.

> >
> > regress_code_simple = """
> > data {
> > int<lower = 0> N; // number of observations
> > real counts[N]; // response variable
> > real time[N]; // predictor variable
> > }
> > parameters {
> > real<lower=0> rate1;
> > real<lower=rate1> rate2;
> > real<lower=rate2> rate3;
>
> Easier to just do
>
> positive_ordered[3] rate;
>
> > real<lower=0> sigma; // standard deviation
> > }
> > transformed parameters {
> > real mu[N]; // fitted values
> > for(i in 1:N)
> > mu[i] = 0.4*exp(-rate1*time[i])+3.0/10*exp(-rate2*time[i])+3.0/10*exp(-rate3*time[i]);
>
> This can be vectorized as follows:
>
> mu = 0.4 * exp(-rate1 * time)
> + 0.3 * exp(-rate2 * time)
> + 0.3 * exp(-rate3 * time));
>
> if you declare time as a vector:
>
> vector[N] time;
>
> But the bigger problem is that it's not going to be identified because
> you've introduced essentially three regression-like coefficient based
> on the same coefficient and you've given the first two rates plenty of
> latitude.
>
> > }
> > model {
> > real alpha;
> > real beta;
> > alpha = 1.0;
> > beta = 1.0;
> >
> >
> >
> > sigma ~ gamma(alpha,beta);
>
> Much better to just do
>
> sigma ~ gamma(1, 1);
>
> >
> > rate1 ~ normal(0,5)T[0,];
> > rate2 ~ normal(9,5)T[0,];
> > rate3 ~ normal(95,10)T[0,];
>
> This isn't the right truncations to normalize:
>
> rate[1] ~ normal(0, 5) T[0, ];
> rate[2] ~ normal(9, 5) T[rate[1], 0];
> rate[3] ~ normal(95, 10) T[rate[2], 0];
>
> You can drop the first truncation for efficiency, but you need
> the next two because they depend on parameters.
>
> > counts ~ normal(mu,sigma);
>
> But I have no idea why you'd do this. If you want to define a mixture,
> I'd suggest looking at the mixture modeling section of the manual. You

>
>
> > }
